prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength cancel the lattice light shift, and for bringing it to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B030 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and the first round has strengthened rather than weakened my reasons. The core is a clear piece of atomic physics: at the magic wavelength the ground and clock states shift equally in the trapping light, so one gets the Doppler-free, recoil-free confinement of an ion with the signal-to-noise of thousands of atoms at once. Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and his first Sr lattice spectroscopy carry the originality. The Boulder programme, built on Ye's strontium clocks and their stability and many-body physics, is what turned this into a 10^-18 instrument. Independent laboratories in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere reproduce each other's frequencies, and those comparisons are the strongest evidence for maturity that any candidate on our list has. It also does what a good basic result does: it lets people ask questions that were out of reach, such as redshift resolved over a millimetre, bounds on drifting constants and the dark-matter searches. I accept that the last items are so far bounds and not detections. I now regard the pending redefinition of the second as a matter of timing and not of merit.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is the one several colleagues put as discovery versus invention. The lattice clock does not show a new phenomenon in nature; it is a new way to use a known one, and the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single quantum systems sit close by. My answer is that the committee has to be honest about what is new. The ingredient is the magic-wavelength trap that makes a many-atom clock possible without losing accuracy, which neither the comb nor the Al+ and Ca+ ion work contained, so the citation must name that and nothing broader. Even so, a committee that wants a new state of matter or a new particle this year could reasonably choose B058 over this, and I would not call that unreasonable. Priority is the second weakness. Lemonde's group at SYRTE, the early NIST/JILA collaborations and Takamoto as a co-author of the key Nature paper all made early contributions, and I cannot rule out from memory that an expert report would sharpen the share between the two names. Third, my own closeness to the field cuts both ways: I may be too generous about how clean the physics is.

responses.point: Kroll agrees with the two-person credit but presses on the share between Katori and Ye, saying the 1e-18 and many-body results that made the clock a tool come mostly from Boulder, and that he would not accept a citation implying the idea alone is the discovery.
responses.response: I think he is right, and I have changed my wording because of it. The round-1 citation I proposed was close to a description of the instrument; the new one says invention and realisation, so it carries both steps. As I read the record, the magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstration of lattice spectroscopy are Katori's, with Takamoto as a junior co-author whom the three-name rule does not let us name. The jump from the 10^-16 range to 10^-18, the control of blackbody and lattice light shifts to that level, and the use of a degenerate Fermi gas as a many-body clock are largely the Boulder group under Ye. Neither step alone is the achievement, and I would present the two roles as complementary and of comparable weight, not as a ranking of one over the other. I add one caution: the effective-priority claim for Boulder rests partly on the comb link, and that overlaps with 2005. It should show up as a reason the clock works, not as a credit to Hall.

responses.point: Olsson, who moved B030 from eighth to first partly on my atomic-physics reading, asks me to say whether Katori's proposal and early Sr demonstration carry the originality or whether Ye's many-body and comb-linked work is of equal weight, and whether Lemonde's group has a real claim.
responses.response: I will answer as plainly as I can, and I would still want an external expert check. The originality in the strict sense is Katori's: the trap-at-magic-wavelength idea and the first demonstration are his, and without them there is no lattice clock for Ye to improve. Lemonde's group and others reproduced and extended these early results within a short time, which shows the idea was real and the physics robust, but I do not read it as an independent invention. The many-body work and the 10^-18 level are of equal weight in my judgement, because that is the point at which the lattice clock became an instrument others use, and Ye's group took it there. So I would not say the pair is clean in the sense of having no other contributors; I would say it is defensible as the two decisive steps. If an expert report shows that Lemonde or Takamoto have a primary, independent claim to the magic-wavelength idea itself, I would want to hear it before the final ballot.

responses.point: Mehlig says broad opening support is not the same as scientific priority, that a universal statistical mechanism like KPZ deserves a hearing even with one advocate, and that he is content to see B030 win but not before the attribution argument for B049 is tested.
responses.response: I agree that support counts do not settle science, and I have tried not to lean on them: my case for B030 stands on the physics and on reproduction between laboratories. I also take his case for KPZ seriously as physics; exact exponents tied to Tracy-Widom statistics and an unexpected breadth are exactly the kind of surprise I like, and I defer to him in statistical mechanics. But the attribution test he asks for is, I think, the one B049 does not pass this year. The 1986 paper has three authors and Parisi, who was recognised in 2021, would be omitted, and Spohn's exact-solution programme is a distinct achievement that a three-name rule cannot absorb comfortably. I would also say that the strict experimental realisations are far fewer than the theory's reach. If he still wants B049 first, I would rather hear how the Kardar-Zhang pair could be worded without splitting the trio, since that is the issue on which I could be persuaded.

responses.point: Eriksson, who now prefers B030 with B058 and B057 as alternatives, says the strength of calculation and measurement together is also why some will call this refined atomic physics rather than a new phenomenon, and that he would not object if the committee valued a new state of matter over an instrument.
responses.response: That concern is fair and I do not want to wave it away. Magic-wavelength conditions do depend on accurate polarizabilities, and theory and experiment have supported each other here, which is how I would expect a mature precision field to look. I do not think it makes the result incremental, because the idea of engineering a trap in which the light shift cancels was not a refinement of an existing clock; it was a different architecture. Still, he and I are on the same side of one point: B058 is a serious alternative, and the missing credit for Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and for the 3D work is what keeps it from being my first choice, not any doubt about the physics. If the committee were to decide that this year should honour a new state of matter, I would want that attribution settled before a final ballot and not afterwards.

uncertainties: Whether an expert report on priority finds that Lemonde's group, Takamoto or others have an independent claim to the magic-wavelength idea or the first lattice clock, which could change the two-name credit.

Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement invention as the discovery or invention in the statutory sense, and whether the citation can be written so that it clearly differs from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
How much weight the not yet realised redefinition of the second and the constant and dark-matter bounds should carry; I treat them as context and not as the basis of the prize.
Whether B058 could be given a fair three-person split; I would reconsider my ranking if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission were resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of those people is credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have no personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye, Takamoto or Lemonde in my profile; my closeness to B030 is disciplinary, as an atomic theorist who knows the physics of the clock and the polarizability calculations behind magic wavelengths. I have no recusal to propose, but I have said that I may be biased upward, and I would accept that the committee weighs my view on B030 accordingly.
